newsitem.title: KENYA: Missing refugee puzzle unsolved in central Africa.
newsitem.headline: Missing refugee puzzle unsolved in central Africa.

text.p: Now you see them, at least some of them, now you don't see anyone at all.

Weeks of reconnaissance, a pile of anecdotal evidence and a heavy dose of speculation have failed to solve the big puzzle of central Africa -- what has become of hundreds of thousands of Rwandans displaced by fighting in eastern Zaire in October?
More than 640,000 of the refugees did go home to Rwanda but the United Nations says there were originally about 1.2 million in Zaire, leaving more than half a million unaccounted for.
Are they wandering through the forests of Zaire, picking fruit off the trees and digging roots from the ground, like hunter gatherers in a latterday Garden of Eden?
Or are they struggling to survive, hungry, exhausted, feverish with malaria and terrified of the fate they might meet if they fall into the wrong hands?
Is the Interahamwe, the Hutu extremist militia, herding them along as a human shield against anyone who tries to repatriate the militiamen for trial on charges of genocide in 1994?
How are relations between them and the local Zairean population, who may not welcome an influx of strangers?

And what future do they have, assuming no one can persuade them to go back to Rwanda? Can they settle safely in Zaire, given the hostile attitude of the government in Kinshasa towards Rwandan immigants, or will they end up in new refugee camps, further from the border?

The United Nations, Western air forces and the independent aid agencies have answered some of these questions for some groups of refugees in some places but they remain very far from turning the scraps of information into a coherent picture.
One of the biggest obstacles is the very terrain across which the refugees have dispersed -- a tropical rain forest of the thickest kind, thinly populated and with few roads.
People on aerial reconnaissance cannot see what is beneath the canopy of trees. Ash from an active volcano close to the Rwandan border has also reduced visibility.

Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, the Canadian commander of a multinational force based in the Ugandan capital Kampala, says U.S. and British reconnaisance planes have scoured a strip of land 150 km (90 miles) wide and several hundred km (miles) long in search of the missing refugees.
The reconnaissance teams last came up with an estimate of 165,000 refugees in that area, hundreds of thousands short of the number who supposedly went missing.
But now it emerges that many others have wandered west of that strip, some more than 200 km (120 miles) from the camps where they were living in October.
The International Red Cross (ICRC) found a group of them at the town of Shabunda on Sunday and said they were in poor condition, stricken with diarrhoea, malaria and malnutrition.
"There are indications that large groups of women, children and elderly people are in the surrounding forest regions under very difficult living conditions," a Red Cross report said.
U.N. sources said on Wednesday that a U.N. flight reckoned to find about 50,000 of them in the Shabunda area. The plane landed and some of the refugees said they wanted to go home.
The medical charity Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF) also says that large numbers of refugees have moved westwards, despite the ravages of malaria and a shortage of food in the area.
Baril painted a rather rosier picture at the weekend, implicitly dismissing the pessimism of the aid agencies.
Speaking of a large group of refugees about 60 km (40 miles) west of the Rwandan border, he said:

"Nature is so luxuriant in that place that these people are, certainly not in good conditions, but they seem to be living off the land like so many thousands and thousands of Zairois. It's quite good land for fruit and vegetables."
"They look in fairly good shape, there's no sign of famine...and no sign they are harshly controlled, either by the Interahamwe or the rebels," he added.

Nicholas Louis of MSF in the northeast Zairean city of Kisangani told Reuters that local people seemed to have abandoned their villages along the Lubutu-Walikale road, apparently one of the main axes for Rwandans in flight.
The Rwandans, mainly peasant farmers from a highly populated country, would find it hard to survive in the unfamiliar rain forest and have little resistance to the malaria, he added.
One ominous sign is that few children are visible along the road but Louis declined to speculate where they might be.
